subject: Biology
title: Invasive Species
description: A micro-lesson that makes Invasive Species usable.

hook.text: When a species arrives somewhere new with no predators, it can multiply out of control.

buildup.text: Cane toads were brought to Australia to eat beetles. They ate everything else instead.

discovery.text: Invasive species outcompete natives for food and space, often driving them toward extinction.

twist.text: Burmese pythons released in Florida's Everglades have decimated native mammal populations.

climax.text: Invasive species cost the global economy over $400 billion a year in damage and control efforts.

punchline.text: Wrong species, wrong place, massive damage.

quiz.question: Why are invasive species so harmful to new environments?
options: They lack natural predators and outcompete natives

details.summary: Invasive species are non-native organisms that spread aggressively in new environments, outcompeting native species. Freed from their natural predators and diseases, invaders like kudzu, cane toads, and zebra mussels cause billions in economic damage and drive native extinctions.
details.whyItMatters: Invasive species are the second-largest driver of biodiversity loss after habitat destruction. They cost the global economy over $400 billion annually and have caused hundreds of documented extinctions worldwide.
takeaways: Invasive species thrive because they lack natural enemies in new habitats
Islands are especially vulnerable to invasion due to naive native species
Prevention through biosecurity is far cheaper than controlling established invaders

faq.question: Why are islands so vulnerable to invasive species?
faq.answer: Island species evolved in isolation without exposure to continental predators, diseases, and competitors. They often lack defensive behaviors or immunity. Introduced rats, cats, and snakes have devastated island bird populations that never evolved to cope with such threats.

faq.question: Can invasive species ever be completely eradicated?
faq.answer: From small islands, yes, through intensive trapping, hunting, or targeted poisons. On continents, eradication is nearly impossible for established invaders. Management focuses on containment and reducing impacts rather than elimination.
